summary: Monday sales team meeting run by Chris Klevan with both closers, Ben Byrne and Andrew Musial, and both setters, Kyla Louie and Kim Forbes-Sobers. Opens on wins — Ben's first paid-in-full close, Andrew's two weekend deals — then a coaching block on tying goals to identity so the $6,000 has a gap big enough to justify it, and a long scripted role-play of the 'will this actually work for me' objection built around the claim that results are guaranteed biology. Moves into projections: Andrew three units and $7,200 cash against target, $3,600 pushed forward; Ben one unit at 6K with $4,800 moved to week four; Kim 20 sets at 79.6% show rate, targeted at 25; Kyla six units targeted at three units and 25 sets. Chris then chases CRM hygiene — every booked call must have a custom activity logged in Close — and sends the setters to a breakout. The remainder is a call review of Andrew's prospect Manny, a Blue Origin technical project manager and Air Force reservist with a pre-diabetes diagnosis and family history, cut short when Chris has to leave. After Chris drops, Ben and Andrew continue talking on the recording.
notable: AFTER THE MANAGER LEAVES THE CALL, both closers mock prospects' sexual orientation on the recording. Ben: 'sorry, this program is not for you. I mean, if you start working out again and get your T-levels fixed, you might go back to your wife. Just kidding. Wow, do you think that you turned gay because you haven't been working out that much?' Andrew: 'Why are you gay?' Ben repeats it, then adds of the Puerto Rican prospect, 'So that explains the gay thing.' This is the single most serious item in the batch and it is captured on a company recording.

An unlisted offer tier is in active use and endorsed by the manager: Andrew 'got him on a Love It or Leave It', a one-month entry he expects to convert — 'I believe after a month he will go for a full six months.' Chris treats it as a standing tool with a limit: 'love it or leave it is definitely something you can use in your back pocket for somebody who has sort of like trust issues within themselves with us... that's where I start to draw the line with the love it or leave it, if we're just offering it to everybody.'

The manager coaches guaranteed-outcome language as a standard rebuttal: 'we know it's science at the end of the day... If they eat the foods and they do the work. The result has to happen. It's human biology. It has to happen' and 'don't show any sort of uncertainty in yourself. Like have full conviction that we get results.'

The manager scripts a misrepresentation of the closer's own incentive: 'it's literally my job to make sure that I don't let people in that we can't help. Because if you come into this and you don't get results... I'm not getting paid for that either.' Closers are paid on the close.

An unconditional refund is scripted with no terms and then immediately steered away from: 'we're not going to hold your money or hold you in here if you can't get the result. But we're not even going to go down that path.'

CRM data integrity is broken at source. Chris: 'if you have a sales call, even if anybody that's booked on your calendar, whether the call happened or didn't happen, a custom activity needs to be updated inside of Close, every single one of them.' Ben: 'In theory, yeah, I just have to do it, I guess. I've never really used those.' No-shows, reschedules and outcomes are therefore missing for Ben's entire tenure.

Ben raises vegetarian fit as an open question — 'it's almost like an objection that has come up twice now with vegetarian people... a lot of it's based off of eating a lot of meat' — and gets only 'We've worked with clients that are vegetarian. There's ways around it.' He had already assured a prospect two days earlier that the protocol is fully customised for vegetarians and vegans.

Ben's account of his own kettlebell use — 'the day before, I'm like, maybe I'll start doing some kettlebell workouts' — sits awkwardly against the personal results story he told a prospect the previous day about mobility fixing his knees after one session.

Setter projection pressure recurs. Kyla is talked from four sets to five by the manager claiming to have misheard: 'Four sets? Five. Four. I heard five. I think I heard five.' Same pattern as the 06/05 meeting with Kim.
Set quality is self-reported as mixed: Kim says 'there was a couple that I set that shouldn't have been set with hindsight', relevant to any show-rate or close-rate denominator.

Unit economics visible in the projections: Andrew's three units produced $7,200 cash against a target implying roughly $3,600 cash per unit, well below the $6,000 six-month price — consistent with routine deposits, instalments or partial collections.

Ben describes his own pre-call routine and a Friday-night episode: 'before I closed that Frank guide, I went and did like a 10 minute letting go meditation' and 'I got a little too open on Saturday, but anyway... Wait, I meant Friday night.'

Andrew describes a prospect in ethnic shorthand — 'he was so freaking Silicon Valley engineer, analytical Indian guy' — and the manager builds the rebuttal around it rather than correcting the framing.
